questions.q: What is the four-step loop a Tier 1 analyst runs on every alert in the queue?
options: Alert fires, SIEM classifies it automatically, no analyst review needed
Alert fires, analyst escalates it automatically, then moves to the next one
Alert fires, analyst reviews it, classifies it, then takes an initial action
Alert fires, analyst deletes it, writes a report, then closes the ticket
questions.explain: Fire, review, classify, act is the repeatable loop this lesson describes -- and review means checking the underlying data, not just the alert label.

questions.q: What is a benign true positive, and how is it different from a false positive?
options: It's the same thing as a false positive, just a different name
It's an alert that automatically escalates to Tier 2 without review
It's an alert that accurately describes real activity that turns out to be legitimate, not malicious -- a false positive is an alert that is simply wrong about what happened
It's an alert that was never reviewed by an analyst
questions.explain: A benign true positive is accurate about what happened -- the activity is real -- but the activity itself isn't malicious, unlike a false positive where the described activity didn't actually happen as described.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, what made the 3am login with a failed MFA-device-add attempt a true positive rather than a benign true positive?
options: It happened at a different SIEM than the first alert
The analyst guessed it was worse without checking any data

The underlying pattern -- unusual time, unfamiliar location, and a follow-on attempt to add an MFA device -- pointed to malicious activity, unlike the conference-travel login confirmed by an IT ticket
True positives and benign true positives are classified identically
questions.explain: Both alerts were accurate about what happened, but checking the underlying data showed one was a legitimate travel login and the other showed signs of an actual account-takeover attempt.

questions.q: Why does slow alert triage matter, according to this lesson?
options: Every minute an alert sits untouched gives a real attacker, if there is one, more dwell time to operate undetected
SIEMs automatically resolve alerts that sit too long
Slow triage only matters for false positives, not true positives
Slow triage has no real impact as long as the alert is eventually reviewed
questions.explain: Dwell time -- how long an attacker operates before being found -- grows directly with how long alerts sit unreviewed in the queue.

questions.q: What are the two failure modes this lesson describes when triage accuracy slips?
options: There is only one failure mode: escalating too much
Classifying too many alerts as benign true positives and too few as false positives
Reviewing alerts too carefully and taking too long to close the queue
Waving off real alerts without checking the data (missing true positives), and escalating everything "just in case" (burning Tier 2's time and training the team to ignore escalations)
questions.explain: Both failure modes come from skipping the review step -- guessing at a classification instead of checking what the underlying data actually shows.
